strand_a.title: Hashtags and handshakes: diplomacy in the age of platforms
strand_a.summary: Rebecca Adler-Nissen argues that diplomacy, historically built on discretion, closed rooms and carefully timed statements, has absorbed digital platforms and with them pressures to be first, visible and credited. She notes concrete consequences, including leaks from sensitive negotiations on sanctions that allowed targets to prepare countermeasures. The piece treats relations between diplomats and technology companies as a new arena where visibility, influence and geopolitical power intersect, and frames science diplomacy within it. It is an interpretive essay in the ERC's magazine. The European research-and-innovation connection is indirect, which is why admission is left for human judgement.

It will support 20 to 30 projects with up to 100 percent funding of eligible costs, including a retroactive clause covering expenses incurred up to three months before the call closes.

strand_a.title: How to Operationalise a Transatlantic Cyber Policy Research Initiative (TCPRI)
strand_a.summary: The EU and US agreed in 2016 to create a Transatlantic Cyber Policy Research Initiative, but three years later the commitment remained largely on paper. This paper takes up the idea and works out how it could actually be run: who convenes it, how researchers and policymakers connect, and what working methods suit a fast-changing threat landscape. It also argues the initiative would work better inside a shared transatlantic strategy for cybersecurity policy research built on existing EU and US science diplomacy. The proposals are the author's design, not an adopted arrangement.

strand_b.title: AI adoption as technology transfer: an integrative review and conceptual framework for governance, validation and knowledge preservation
strand_b.authors: Musarat Kabir-Chisty
strand_b.summary: The paper argues that prevailing AI governance frameworks, built on ethics, transparency, risk management and compliance, assume the human processes and expertise being embedded into AI systems have already been captured accurately. It reframes AI adoption as a technology-transfer problem, borrowing from pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, aerospace and advanced manufacturing, where success depends on reproducibility and validation, traceability and knowledge preservation, and process control with continuous verification. To operationalise this it introduces the AI Technology Transfer Framework, a seven-stage governance model for moving workflows, expertise and decision-making into AI systems while retaining accountability and organisational memory. It is a conceptual framework from an integrative review, not an empirically tested method.

strand_b.title: FAIR-Compute: A Roadmap for Fair and Efficient Allocation of Federated Digital Research Infrastructure
strand_b.authors: Konstantinos E. Zachariadis, Ahmed Sayed, Dimitris Fotakis, Angeliki Mathioudaki, Wan Shuen Siaw
strand_b.source: arXiv (final report to the National Federated Compute Services Flexible Fund)
strand_b.summary: The report was produced for the UK National Federated Compute Services Flexible Fund, combining stakeholder interviews, a demand-side survey, a literature review and a simulation study to examine how federated research computing is actually allocated. It maps infrastructure tiers and federation models, then examines occupancy, utilisation and the economic case to identify where allocation breaks down. The analytical core is a model of HPC allocation covering jobs, a descriptive scheduler, strategic reporting by users and offline welfare comparisons, with allocation treated as routing under congestion. Recommendations for the NFCS roadmap follow. The mechanisms are modelled and simulated rather than deployed, and the empirical base centres on the UK system with international comparison.
strand_b.core_message: Allocation failures, not just capacity limits, drive poor utilisation of federated research computing; a mechanism-design model with strategic reporting and welfare metrics offers a systematic alternative.

strand_b.title: Industrial policy and technology linkages: Conceptualizing China’s approach
strand_b.authors: Robin Schindowski, Jeroen Groenewegen-Lau, Max J. Zenglein
strand_b.source: KU Leuven VIVES (VIVES Discussion Paper No. 107)
strand_b.summary: The paper proposes a schematic framework for analysing industrial policy, developed from a systematic review of Chinese-language sources. It distinguishes future industries, high-technology fields of strategic importance with immature markets, from emerging industries that they become once scientific advances yield commercially viable products, and from the large base of traditional industries. Traditional firms adopt emerging technology to upgrade, while providing an initial market that helps emerging firms scale. The authors argue policy concentrates state support on the linkages between these types. Case studies on electric vehicles, textiles and advanced semiconductors show how the framework applies to specific sectors.
strand_b.core_message: Industrial policy can be analysed as targeted support for technology linkages between future, emerging and traditional industry types.

strand_b.title: Bringing Clarity to the Smart City Definition Jungle: Toward an Integrative and a Data-Centric Conceptualization of Urban Systems
strand_b.authors: Christian Anschütz
strand_b.summary: The paper addresses two kinds of fragmentation in smart city research: conceptual disagreement about what a smart city is, and heterogeneity in how smart city architectures are actually built. It systematically synthesises 69 academic definitions and contrasts them with empirical architectural patterns observed in leading European and North American cities. From this it derives an integrative definition conceptualising the smart city as a learning, cyber-socio-technical urban system integrating digital infrastructures and data resources. The contribution is conceptual and architectural rather than empirical: it offers a transferable framework others can apply, not new measurements of any particular city. Its European content is incidental, since the cities studied are used as architectural evidence rather than as a policy subject.

strand_b.title: Country-level innovation performance: introducing sustainable innovation efficiency
strand_b.authors: Yong Tan, Yu Zhao
strand_b.summary: The authors argue that measuring innovation efficiency alone gives an incomplete picture of national innovation performance, and introduce sustainable innovation efficiency to capture how well a country converts research and development inputs into stable outputs when those inputs fluctuate. Using Data Envelopment Analysis on thirty countries from 2009 to 2018, they find overall innovation efficiency is low, with scores consistently below 0.25. High-income countries score better on sustainable innovation efficiency, while lower-middle-income countries score highest on plain innovation efficiency. East Asia and the Pacific outperform Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East and North Africa on innovation efficiency, with variation on the sustainable measure. The construct is new, so its external validity is not yet established.

strand_b.summary: The article rejects the view that foresight methods are transferable tools chosen mainly by object, horizon or data, and builds a framework linking methods to institutional functions across four governance logics: technocratic, market-managerial, networked and anticipatory. The EU is the focal case of institutionalised foresight in a multi-level system, with Japan and South Korea as contrastive cases. Evidence combines exploratory bibliometric mapping of Scopus, VOSviewer semantic analysis of foresight-method terms, manual validation of 68 publications and qualitative case interpretation. strand_b.title: A Multi-agent Approach to Technology Intelligence: From Patents to Market Signals with Large Language Models
strand_b.authors: Jan Černý
strand_b.summary: TechIntel-MAS is an eight-role multi-agent system built on the CrewAI framework that converts disclosed patent filings and a free-text intelligence request into a structured competitive-intelligence report. It treats patents as seed signals and searches the open web for matching market evidence such as products, vendors and partnerships, reporting honestly when none is found. Six frontier models run the generative roles in parallel while a separate evaluator pool operates verifier, telemetry and judge roles, so no model evaluates its own output. The authors report precision, recall, F1, semantic alignment, relevancy and calibration error across four patent filings. This is a pilot study on a small test set.

strand_b.title: Evidence for the future? Strategic foresight as a source of evidence for policymaking
strand_b.authors: Laura De Vito, Gaia Taffoni
strand_b.summary: The article treats strategic foresight as a form of policy evidence and asks under what conditions it can be recognised as legitimate and effective. Because foresight addresses uncertainty and long-term change, its reliability and usability problems differ from those of past-oriented evidence. The authors compare two policy-focused cases: the UK Government Office for Science's Net Zero Society scenarios and pathways report, and the Joint Research Centre's Policy Lab together with the ESPAS horizon scanning exercise. From these they build a framework of three enablers that raise foresight's evidential value. The framework is derived from two diverse cases and is offered for future testing, not validated at scale.
strand_b.core_message: Foresight's evidential value rests on three enablers, and the two cases show these can be observed and compared across institutional settings.
strand_b.relevance_note: A transferable evaluation framework for foresight evidence, with the EU's own foresight machinery as one of the two cases.

strand_b.title: The enrichment of post-growth future alternatives for Europe using an online integral foresight methodology
strand_b.authors: András Márton, Judit Gáspár, Éva Hideg, Attila Szathmári, Gabriella Kiss, Alexandra Köves
strand_b.summary: Post-growth covers economic models such as degrowth, doughnut economics and wellbeing economics that aim for development within planetary limits rather than expanding output. The method the authors call integral foresight combines a review of literature on possible futures with horizon scanning and scenario building, run as multiple online rounds among researchers, subject experts and futurists. The output is a filtered, refined and categorised set of futures statements spanning social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal, ethical and demographic dimensions, plus scenarios built on differing assumptions. The conclusions are expert expectations elicited through a structured process, not forecasts or evidence about what will occur. Participants were recruited for their engagement with post-growth and sustainability, which shapes the range of views represented.

strand_b.title: Anticipating return migration to Ukraine: participatory foresight with Ukrainians displaced to Spain
strand_b.authors: Oksana Udovyk, Ruth M-Domènech
strand_b.summary: This study engaged twenty displaced Ukrainians living in Valencia between May and December 2023 in a participatory foresight process about possible return migration. The process combined workshops, online messaging group discussions, interviews and participatory observation, and ended with an open art exhibition. Participants carried out a collective horizon scan, identifying weak signals and emerging trends, then examined critical uncertainties and built scenarios from them. The methodological point is that people directly affected by an uncertain future acted as the foresight practitioners rather than as subjects. The sample is small and situated in one host city, so the scenarios describe how this group anticipates return rather than forecasting actual return flows.

strand_b.title: From blur to blueprint: a fuzzy delphi methodology for evaluating early-stage emerging technologies—the case of end-of-life automotive traction battery disassembly
strand_b.authors: Max Rettenmeier, Mauritz Möller, Alexander Sauer
strand_b.summary: The authors tackle a recurring problem: choosing between emerging technologies when there is almost no quantitative performance data. They built the criteria from the ground up, identifying fourteen stakeholder groups and running 65 interviews to derive sixteen evaluation criteria. Two Delphi panels then weighted the criteria and scored each technology, with fuzzy logic used to absorb the disagreement between experts. Applied to dismantling end-of-life electric vehicle batteries, the procedure singled out laser cutting and shredding. The case is a validation exercise: the contribution the authors claim is the method itself, which they argue transfers to other early-stage technology domains.

strand_b.title: Bias in Expert Judgment Within Large‐Scale Science and Technology Delphis: What Do We Know (and Not Know) and Can Utilization of Panelists' Rationales Help Reduce Potential Bias?
strand_b.authors: Xinyu Jiang, Ian Belton, George Wright
strand_b.summary: A 2025 paper argued that expert judgments in large science and technology Delphi surveys are systematically biased. This article disputes that. It argues the original authors misread what Delphi is for, conflated disagreement with bias, and analysed secondary data without sufficient rigour. In place of that diagnosis it proposes a cleaner design: distinguish legitimate differences of opinion between experts and non-experts from genuine cognitive or motivational bias, and treat the reasons panelists write for their answers as the primary material for both practice and controlled study. The contribution is a research design, not new survey results.
strand_b.core_message: The bias claims do not hold, because the underlying analysis conflates expert-non-expert divergence with bias and lacks rigour; rationale-based designs are proposed instead.
strand_b.relevance_note: Offers a transferable improvement to how Delphi-based foresight studies are designed and evaluated.

strand_b.title: Enhancing regulatory foresight through weak signal mining: An AI-based micro-topic emergence scoring approach
strand_b.authors: Axel Menning, Zsuzsa Farkas, Krisztián Vribék, Bas van der Velden
strand_b.summary: Emerging risks in food and feed safety often manifest through weak, ambiguous signals long before they reach regulatory attention. This paper presents the Weak Signal Miner (WSM), an AI-based, end-to-end pipeline for detecting such early-stage signals within large text corpora. The method combines transformer-based micro-topic modelling, adaptive temporal aggregation, and a recency-and-magnitude scoring scheme to ide. Enhancing regulatory foresight through weak signal mining: An AI-based micro-topic emergence scoring approach. Retrospective analyses demonstrate the tool’s effectiveness: the WSM surfaces signals related to Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) contamination (2004–2007) and citrinin in red yeast rice supplements (2010–2017) well before their formal recognition in an EFSA (European Food Safety Authority) opinion.

strand_b.title: Horizon Scanning Methods for Health Care Technology Innovation Identification: Rapid Scoping Review of Patent Research Studies
strand_b.authors: Sonia Garcia Gonzalez-Moral, Erin Pennock, Olushola Ewedairo, Elizabeth Green, James Elgey, Andrew Mkwashi
strand_b.summary: The review comes from the NIHR Innovation Observatory, the UK national horizon-scanning body, and surveys studies that use patent data to identify emerging health technologies. It asks which intellectual-property sources are used, by what retrieval and analysis methods, and for what purpose, identifying up to 47 patent databases with just over a quarter of studies using more than one. Most studies relied on patent databases alone, trend analysis was the most common objective, and a third used automated approaches, often with network visualisation tools. The authors warn that inconsistent deduplication risks inflating results and call for greater transparency and rigour. The review maps practice rather than testing which method detects innovation earliest.

strand_b.title: Anticipatory Methods for the Emergence of Radically New Technologies: Navigating Uncertainty
strand_b.authors: Barbara L. van Veen, J. Roland Ortt
strand_b.summary: Radically new technologies are difficult to anticipate because the usual forecasting inputs, such as stable trends and established markets, do not yet exist. This article works through the characteristics that mark such emergence: novelty, meaning significant departure from the state of the art; growth in actors, funding and patents; coherence, as research lines converge and a community of practice forms; potential impact across socio-economic systems and disciplines; and persistent uncertainty. It uses these to reason about which anticipatory methods are appropriate at which stage. The contribution is conceptual guidance for navigating uncertainty rather than an empirical test showing that the resulting method choices produce better anticipation.

strand_b.title: Governing emerging technologies—looking forward with horizon scanning and looking back with technology audits
strand_b.authors: Henry T. Greely
strand_b.summary: Technology governance debate, especially in the life sciences, tends to concentrate on limits to research and on whether to permit wide use. This article argues that two stages receive far less attention: anticipating technologies with important effects before they arrive, and monitoring the actual effects of technologies once adopted. It proposes a visible and influential Horizon Scanning Group to spot and analyse emerging technologies, and more formal Technology Audit Groups to assess developments after deployment. A third section works through the organisational questions such bodies raise, including mandate and composition, and suggests specific approaches. The article is a governance proposal; neither body existed, so there is no evidence of how they would perform in practice.

strand_b.title: Co-creating climate-resilient cities: a multi-method participatory approach for future scenario building and prioritization

strand_b.summary: The authors target what they call the vision-to-decision gap, where participatory climate planning produces narratives that formal administration cannot use. Their framework has three parts: co-creative scenario building for 2050 urban futures, quantitative prioritisation using the Analytic Hierarchy Process to weight stakeholder-defined criteria, and expert-led feedback loops to check technical feasibility. It was deployed in two European Living Labs with contrasting conditions, the Mediterranean island of Chios in Greece and Vilnius in Lithuania. strand_b.title: Macrohistorical Cycle Synchronization as a Method for Long‐Range Foresight: The Ten Mega Epochs Model
strand_b.authors: Tuomo Kuosa
strand_b.summary: Most foresight looks a decade or two ahead. This article proposes a method for looking much further. It synthesises five nested cycles — from decadal innovation waves up to century-long institutional rhythms — and argues that they periodically fall into step, producing what the author calls a Mega Epoch about every 250 years. The method is demonstrated by mapping 2,500 years of Western history into ten such epochs, drawing on macrohistorians including Ibn Khaldun, Toynbee, Kondratieff, Strauss and Howe, and Turchin. The author states the framework is non-deterministic, open to falsification, and dependent on assumptions such as stable generation length.

strand_b.reader_more: This paper examines what happens when randomly selected citizens are integrated into a formal exploratory scenario process, an approach less studied than participatory scenario work generally. strand_b.summary: Financial systems under heavy institutional and geopolitical constraint are hard to forecast with conventional tools. This study builds a foresight framework around the Futures Triangle, which sets future-oriented goals against present pressures and inherited institutional limits. It adds a fuzzy multi-criteria step that scores candidate drivers on importance, uncertainty and rate of change, making the reduction from a long driver list to a working set explicit rather than tacit. strand_b.title: A comparison of two methods for expert elicitation in health technology assessments
strand_b.authors: Bogdan Grigore, Jaime Peters, Christopher Hyde, Ken Stein
strand_b.summary: When data needed for decision-model parameters are missing, formal elicitation of expert judgement can characterise the uncertainty. The authors asked clinical experts to express judgements as probability distributions using two methods, the histogram and the hybrid approach, presented in random order, within a prostate cancer cost-effectiveness model. Distributions were aggregated with and without weighting and fed into probabilistic analysis, and using expert opinion cut the expected value of perfect information at the thirty thousand pound per QALY threshold by 74 to 86 percent. Experts found the histogram method easier but felt the hybrid method captured their views more accurately. Only six of twenty-seven invited experts completed the task, which limits the comparison.
strand_b.core_message: The two elicitation methods produced broadly similar decision conclusions, while including expert opinion markedly reduced decision uncertainty.
strand_b.relevance_note: A transferable evaluation design for expert elicitation, relevant wherever expert judgement feeds quantitative assessment.

strand_b.title: Anticipatory Data Governance in the Age of AI: Emerging Signals in Data Access, Reuse, and Sovereignty
strand_b.authors: Adam Zable, Stefaan Verhulst
strand_b.summary: Two decades of open-data policy assumed that reuse is visible and traceable, that institutions keep meaningful control over information flows, and that humans read the data. This paper argues generative and inferential AI breaks all three: data disappears into opaque training pipelines, sensitive knowledge can be generated without touching the underlying dataset, and machines are becoming the main producers and consumers of information. The findings come from two expert forecasting studios convened by The GovLab in 2025-2026 with nineteen senior practitioners across statistics, trade policy, open science, AI governance and geospatial systems, whose elicited signals were clustered and stress-tested. Seven convergent signals are identified.

strand_b.title: Foresight prototyping: developing an evaluation framework and strategy for future-oriented design
strand_b.authors: Jiayue Wang, Lin Zhu, Jiawei Li
strand_b.summary: Foresight prototyping uses speculative artefacts to explore possible futures and support anticipatory design thinking, but studio critique of such artefacts has lacked shared evaluation criteria. Drawing on a literature review, author interviews and quantitative analysis of perceptual ratings, the study identifies four dimensions: functional visibility, sensory experience, future adaptability and creative divergence. These form the Foresight Prototype Evaluation Framework, intended to support consistent, evidence-based assessment and feedback. The authors note the framework is validated in an educational studio context and argue it should transfer to professional design review, but that professional validation, including comparison against existing review routines, is future work.

strand_b.summary: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism requires product-level, facility-specific emissions data, which collides with suppliers' unwillingness to expose production detail. The authors propose a reference architecture using the International Data Spaces framework so that environmental telemetry can be exchanged verifiably without ceding control of the underlying data. They separate mandatory CBAM obligations from voluntary Science Based Targets commitments and from Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design requirements. A prospective roadmapping method is introduced to turn upstream physical dependencies into feedback loops, illustrated on the Taipei-Penang semiconductor corridor. The work is a design proposal and roadmap; it reports no deployment or evaluation.

strand_b.title: Delphi method applicability in drug foresight
strand_b.authors: Tomi Lintonen, Karoliina Karjalainen, Sanna Rönkä, Elina Kotovirta, Solja Niemelä
strand_b.source: Substance Abuse Treatment, Prevention, and Policy
strand_b.summary: A Delphi panel conducted in Finland between 2009 and 2011 made predictions about drug use, markets, legislation and care. The authors test those predictions against what actually happened by 2020, using published statistics, survey results, official registers, wastewater analyses and official documents, cross-checking sources where possible. Experts correctly foresaw rising drug use, rising approval of drug use and the absence of legislative change, and correctly anticipated more lenient enforcement toward users and the merging of mental health and addiction care. They were wrong about a surge in new synthetic drugs and did not anticipate stable unit prices or rising buprenorphine misuse. The authors conclude that continuation of existing trends is easier to foresee than discontinuity.
strand_b.core_message: Delphi experts predicted the continuation of existing trends accurately but failed to anticipate discontinuities in drug markets and substance popularity.

strand_b.title: A structured expert judgement elicitation approach: how can it inform sound intervention decision-making to support household food security?
strand_b.authors: Sue Kleve, Martine J Barons
strand_b.summary: Decisions about household food security often depend on quantities for which no reliable data exist. This study examines structured expert judgement elicitation as a way to produce robust, defensible estimates for three determinants: food cost, household disposable income and physical access, feeding a proof-of-concept decision support system. It implements the Investigate, Discuss, Estimate, Aggregate protocol with both quantitative and qualitative elements, across pre- and post-activity work and a one-day face-to-face workshop supported by briefing materials. The authors argue that informal expert panels are prone to social deference, availability bias and semantic misunderstanding, producing results that are often unreproducible, and that structured approaches mitigate these. The protocol itself is established; its use in high-income household food security is what the authors present as novel.
strand_b.core_message: The IDEA elicitation protocol yielded usable, defensible estimates for three food security determinants and can supply inputs to a decision support system where data are otherwise missing.

strand_b.title: Which biodiversity futures? Towards coherent design choices for scenarios exploring policy‐relevant questions
strand_b.authors: Anita Lazurko, Sarah Sinclair, Jennifer A. Border, Diana E. Bowler, William H. Morgan, James W. Pearce‐Higgins, Paul Woodcock, Nick J. B. Isaac
strand_b.summary: Decision-makers face pressure to act transformatively on biodiversity loss, and scenarios are used to explore alternative futures and the outcomes of possible actions. The authors argue that amid considerable methodological diversity there is little guidance on the range of scenario design choices available or their suitability for particular applications. That gap produces a fragmented and opaque scenario landscape, hinders interoperability between scenarios, and risks projections or decisions that miss important risks or opportunities for transformative change. In response they develop and validate a framework to support coherent design choices, meaning choices that are intentional, transparent and aligned with the question being asked. The contribution is methodological guidance for scenario builders; it is demonstrated on biodiversity applications, and its wider transferability is argued rather than tested across domains.

strand_b.title: GenAI-Supported strategy development in VUCA scenarios and Multi-GenAI evaluation
strand_b.authors: Engin Yurdasever, Canan Yıldıran
strand_b.summary: The study asks whether generative AI tools differ in strategy development and strategic reasoning across the separate components of volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity, rather than treating VUCA as one undifferentiated condition. It uses an exploratory design combining a qualitative scenario method with strategy development by several generative AI systems and an AI-based evaluation step in which model outputs are assessed comparatively. The design itself is the transferable element, offering a repeatable way to benchmark AI strategic reasoning. The authors note limitations: strategy development was conducted in a single-shot manner, and access to these tools is unevenly distributed across organisations, which constrains how far the findings carry into practice.

strand_b.title: From Theory to Protocol: Executable Frameworks for Creative Emergence and Strategic Foresight
strand_b.authors: Shun Fujiyoshi
strand_b.summary: The paper takes descriptive theories of creativity and foresight, including Koestler's bisociation, de Bono's lateral thinking and Ansoff's weak signals, and converts them into two executable protocols. GHOSTY COLLIDER is a five-step procedure for cross-domain creative emergence through structural de-labelling and collision; PRECOG PROTOCOL is a five-step procedure for signal-based strategic foresight with multi-axis timing judgement. Both specify explicit quality criteria, anti-pattern detection and measurable outputs. Evaluation uses five case studies, controlled comparisons with and without the protocols, and structural analysis. The author states plainly that all case studies were run by a single operator with AI assistance, so the evidence is proof-of-concept and multi-user validation remains outstanding.
strand_b.core_message: Two five-step protocols operationalise bisociation-style creative collision and weak-signal foresight into repeatable procedures with explicit quality criteria and anti-pattern checks.

strand_b.title: AirForesight: Current-to-Future Spatial Map Imagination with Cross-Space Planning Consistency for UAV-VLN
strand_b.authors: Yutong Liu, Xiaojie Li, Mingzhu Xu, Jianlong Wu
strand_b.summary: The paper proposes AirForesight, a framework for unmanned aerial vehicle vision-language navigation, where a drone must follow written instructions and move through complex outdoor space. Existing methods largely map vision and language inputs straight to actions, giving limited explicit grounding in the scene. AirForesight instead learns a structured representation of the current map from multiple viewpoints, supervised jointly by map reconstruction and future-trajectory prediction, then propagates that knowledge to reasoning about future maps. The contribution is a new architecture rather than an application of an existing one. Its relevance to the Radar's notion of reusable method is what requires human judgement.
strand_b.core_message: A framework combining current-map reconstruction with future-trajectory prediction under structured causal attention improves UAV vision-language navigation.

strand_b.title: Backcasting in futures studies: a synthesized scholarly and planning approach to strategic smart sustainable city development
strand_b.authors: Simon Elias Bibri
strand_b.summary: Backcasting starts from a desired future state and works backwards to identify the steps needed to reach it, in contrast to forecasting from present trends. This article argues the approach has developed along two partly separate tracks, one scholarly and one in planning practice, and synthesises them into a single framework aimed at long-horizon strategic development. It applies the synthesis to smart sustainable city development, treating that domain as an instance of operationalising sustainability goals rather than as the sole target. The work is a conceptual and methodological synthesis of existing literature, so it consolidates and structures backcasting practice rather than reporting a new empirical test of it.
strand_b.core_message: Backcasting's scholarly and planning strands can be combined into one operational approach for setting and working back from long-horizon strategic goals.

strand_c.title: Strategic research and innovation centres
strand_c.summary: Innovation Fund Denmark has opened a call under its Strategic Defence Initiative 2026-2029 to establish up to four strategic research and innovation centres in defence technology and security. The total call budget is a minimum of DKK 585 million, with the Fund covering up to 90 per cent of costs. Selection runs in two phases, an expression of interest with a roadmap followed by a full application by invitation. The centres must build on existing Danish research strengths rather than create new ones, and must be broad partnerships spanning research, industry and public authorities. The design is mission-driven with milestone-based tranche funding and go/no-go decisions, and prioritises higher technology readiness levels for rapid application.

strand_c.title: Science Europe presents Practical Guide to Implementing Responsible Research Assessment at RFOs
strand_c.summary: The guide was presented on 21 July 2026 and offers guidance, resources and illustrative examples for funders at different stages: creating a responsible research assessment strategy, reforming existing practices, or moving towards more holistic and inclusive approaches. It is described as discipline-agnostic and adaptable to different organisational contexts, intended to inspire varied approaches rather than prescribe one. It was co-developed by DORA, the Global Research Council's Responsible Research Assessment Working Group and Science Europe, informed by stakeholder discussions including a workshop in Copenhagen in December 2025. It is a companion volume to an equivalent 2025 DORA guide for research performing organisations. This record is a secondary announcement rather than the guide itself.

strand_c.title: ESFRI-EOSC Task Force publishes report on EOSC and Research Infrastructures
strand_c.summary: The joint ESFRI-EOSC Task Force has published a highlights report from a policy workshop held in Milan on 16 and 17 March 2026. Around ninety representatives of research infrastructures, EOSC Nodes, the EOSC Steering Board, the EOSC Association and the European Commission attended to examine how the European Open Science Cloud and the European research infrastructure landscape relate to each other. The report sets out opportunities and challenges around the developing EOSC Federation. Topics covered include visibility of services and resources, sustainability and funding models, onboarding processes, FAIR data practice, community engagement and the role research infrastructures should play. Participants called for stronger communication, clearer onboarding pathways and better cost-benefit analysis.

strand_c.title: European Commission updates EIC Fund Investment Guidelines for the EIC Accelerator and STEP Scaleup
strand_c.authors: European Innovation Council and SMEs Executive Agency
strand_c.summary: These are the 2026 investment guidelines for the European Innovation Council Fund, covering the EIC Accelerator and the STEP Scaleup instrument. The Horizon Europe compartment targets pre-seed, seed and early-stage small firms and small mid-caps with up to 499 employees, aiming at high-risk projects not yet attractive to private investors so that public money de-risks them and draws in private capital. The document defines deep technology as resting on cutting-edge scientific advances, distinguishing it from high technology defined by research intensity alone. Notably, it sets out safeguards to protect EU interests, including acquiring blocking stakes and securing European ownership of intellectual property, and requires that supported companies keep most of their value in the EU or associated countries.
strand_c.core_message: The guidelines codify eligibility and a deep technology definition, and give the fund explicit tools to protect EU interests, including blocking stakes, secondary share purchase and requirements that company value and intellectual property remain in the EU or associated countries.
strand_c.relevance_note: Shows technological sovereignty concerns written directly into the operating rules of the EU's main innovation investment vehicle.

strand_c.title: COM(2026) 504 final - Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on a framework of measures for strengthening the Union's semiconductor ecosystem, repealing Regulation (EU) 2023/1781 (Chips Act 2.0)
strand_c.summary: This is COM(2026) 504 final, adopted on 3 June 2026 under procedure 2026/0139 (COD). It proposes a regulation on a framework of measures for strengthening the Union's semiconductor ecosystem and would repeal Regulation (EU) 2023/1781, the original Chips Act. The explanatory memorandum sets out the context and objectives, and the file is accompanied by impact assessment documents SWD(2026) 504 and SWD(2026) 505. Repealing and replacing the existing regulation is a substantial legal step rather than an amendment. As an ordinary legislative procedure proposal it still requires agreement by the European Parliament and Council before anything takes effect.

strand_c.title: Science Europe calls for stronger minimum standards to improve research careers across Europe
strand_c.summary: Science Europe published a set of recommendations intended to make the European research ecosystem more attractive, supportive and responsive to research talent. They are structured around three interconnected areas: working conditions and employment; research environment; and professional development, wellbeing and supporting infrastructure. The organisation states that the recommendations reflect a common understanding among its member organisations that a shared approach to minimum standards is necessary for continued progress and effective advocacy. Specific elements include fair salaries, robust social security, transparent career pathways and conditions supporting work-life balance. These are recommendations to member organisations rather than binding requirements, so the improvements described are intended rather than achieved.

strand_c.title: Japan officially joins Horizon Europe
strand_c.summary: Japan became officially associated to Horizon Europe on 30 July 2026. With 123 million people it is the most populous country associated to the programme, and the association brings one of the world's most advanced research and innovation systems into the network. The agreement lets Japanese researchers and organisations participate on equal terms with those from EU member states and other associated countries. The announcement frames this as a step in the EU-Japan Strategic Partnership and a shared commitment to open, rules-based international research cooperation, with cooperation expected to expand around the digital transition, health and technologies supporting climate neutrality.

strand_c.title: COM(2026) 502 final - Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a framework of measures for strengthening Europe's cloud and AI ecosystem (Cloud and AI Development Act)
strand_c.summary: This is the Commission's formal legislative proposal, COM(2026) 502 final, adopted on 3 June 2026 under procedure 2026/0138 (COD). It proposes a regulation establishing a framework of measures to strengthen Europe's cloud and artificial intelligence ecosystem. The explanatory memorandum sets out the context and objectives, and the proposal is accompanied by impact assessment documents including SWD(2026) 502 and SWD(2026) 503. As an ordinary legislative procedure file it must still pass the European Parliament and Council, so its provisions are proposed rather than enacted. It is one of the two legislative components of the technological sovereignty package announced the same day.

strand_c.title: EU faces mixed prospects in tech sovereignty, new policy brief finds
strand_c.summary: The brief analyses scientific output, technological performance and trade in critical goods across advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, micro- and nanoelectronics, energy harvesting and life sciences. The EU is comparatively strong and largely sovereign in advanced manufacturing and robotics and retains solid scientific and industrial capacity in life sciences, with robust research competences in micro- and nanoelectronics and energy harvesting. Heavy dependence on imported microchips and Chinese dominance in energy technologies remain material vulnerabilities. In artificial intelligence the EU is weakly positioned overall, with pockets of scientific excellence but high external dependence. The brief argues these patterns reflect long-standing global divisions of labour and calls for a broader concept of sovereignty than import dependence.

strand_c.title: EIC Board calls for faster deployment of deep tech
strand_c.summary: In a statement published on 24 June 2026 the European Innovation Council Board called for faster deployment of European deep tech to strengthen energy resilience. It notes that more than half of EU energy consumption still rests on imported fossil fuels, leaving economic resilience, industrial competitiveness and strategic autonomy exposed. The Board frames this as an opportunity, pointing to nearly 100 companies in the EIC portfolio working across twelve areas of the energy value chain, including generation, storage, hydrogen, renewable fuels, transmission, advanced materials and supply chain resilience. Its argument is that the next challenge is moving these from breakthrough to large-scale industrial deployment. This is an advisory position, not a funding decision.

strand_c.title: Science|Business: Zaharieva hopes for a Horizon Europe deal in 2026
strand_c.summary: In a Science|Business interview of 24 August 2026, EU research commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva said a deal on the next Horizon Europe is needed by the end of 2026 for the programme to run from 1 January 2028, since delay would push back the first calls for proposals due in early 2028. The Council reached a partial agreement in June, with governments seeking more say over priorities. Parliament needed at least two more months before a plenary vote expected at the end of October, after which trilogue talks would begin. Parliament's industry and research rapporteurs had tabled hundreds of amendments. This reports positions and timing, not an agreed outcome.

strand_c.title: European Research Ministers discuss how to maximise R&I contribution to improve Europe’s competitiveness, security and prosperity
strand_c.summary: The informal Competitiveness Council in research configuration met in Dublin on 20 and 21 July 2026, chaired by Ireland's minister James Lawless and attended by Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva, alongside representatives of Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Iceland and Norway. The first debate addressed a genuine single market for knowledge, research and innovation, building on the Letta and Draghi reports and the One Europe, One Market roadmap, and centred on the fifth freedom. The second addressed Europe's innovation gap and the transition from excellent research to competitive companies. This was an informal exchange, so no legal act or Council conclusion was adopted.

strand_c.title: New scoreboard shows success of European startup policies
strand_c.summary: The Commission presented the first European Startup and Scaleup Scoreboard on 29 May 2026. Against a 2020 baseline, 20 of 27 Member States have improved, which the Commission reads as evidence that targeted support for founders drives innovation and growth. The scoreboard uses 36 indicators and links innovation-friendly regulation, access to talent and venture capital to startup performance, with Estonia, Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands and Denmark running 40 to 60 percentage points above the EU average. strand_c.title: European Union and Australia successfully conclude Horizon Europe negotiations
strand_c.summary: On 9 June 2026 the European Commission and Australia concluded negotiations on Australia's association to Horizon Europe. The item records that Australian organisations have taken part in 239 Horizon Europe projects so far, with roughly one in four individual applications selected, a 24.39% success rate. From January 2027 a transitional arrangement moves Australian entities from third-country rules, under which they generally self-funded or relied on narrow exceptions, to treatment as eligible entities from an associated country. That gives them routine access to EU funding under Pillar II on the same terms as Member States, including the ability to lead consortia. Negotiations concluded is not the same as an agreement in force.

strand_c.title: Associated Countries urge EU to keep FP10 open and research-led
strand_c.summary: The Russell Group, U15 Canada, swissuniversities and Universities New Zealand wrote jointly to the Cyprus EU Presidency asking that the tenth framework programme stay open, research-led and attractive to trusted international partners. They describe Horizon Europe as a success for both science and diplomacy and argue that associated countries strengthen its research base. Their specific asks include a research-led Pillar II, continued observer roles for associated countries in governance, protection for fundamental research, a fully independent European Research Council, bottom-up MSCA, minimal topic exclusions and equal treatment in applications. They also want faster association procedures so trusted partners can join from the start.

strand_c.title: ESPI Insights, Issue 73, August 2026
strand_c.summary: ESPI Insights Issue 73 compiles European space sector developments for August 2026. Substantive items include the implementation agreement signed on 7 August between the Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium, moving IRIS2 into full deployment: the constellation grows to 348 satellites, 330 in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium Earth orbit, with programme cost rising roughly 50 percent from 10.55 to 15.6 billion euros and first launches still targeted for 2029. It also records ESA's first European Launcher Challenge contracts with Isar Aerospace, PLD Space and RFA on 27 August, and SES awarding OHB about 1 billion euros for the MEO platforms. The issue is a digest, so each item would normally be a separate record.

strand_c.title: EuroHPC JU Inaugurates Arrhenius, a New Mid-range Supercomputer Together With NAISS in Sweden
strand_c.summary: The EuroHPC Joint Undertaking inaugurated Arrhenius at Linkoping University, with EuroHPC Executive Director Anders Dam Jensen and Swedish State Secretary Maria Nilsson attending the ceremony. The machine is a mid-range system capable of more than 60 petaflops, and it ranked 42nd in the TOP500 list published in June 2026. It is designed for complex simulation and compute-intensive AI work, with intended applications in climate modelling, materials science, life sciences and engineering. The announcement frames the system as a step towards European technological sovereignty. This is an operational deployment rather than a plan, though claims about future scientific breakthroughs are aspirational.

strand_c.title: Six New Quantum Calls Launched by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking
strand_c.summary: The EuroHPC Joint Undertaking opened six calls on 13 August 2026 covering strategic quantum technologies and supporting infrastructure. The trapped-ion topic, HORIZON-JU-EUROHPC-2026-TIPT-09, seeks a full-stack quantum computer with more than a thousand individually addressable physical qubits, integrated with classical high-performance computing and reachable over cloud platforms, with a budget of twenty million euros and projects running three and a half years. A parallel superconducting topic, SPT-10, targets a comparable qubit count using chiplet technology for long coherence times and error correction. Applications close on 17 November 2026. These are calls for proposals, so no projects or results exist yet.

strand_c.title: EU launches AI Gigafactories call to boost Europe's computing capacity
strand_c.summary: On 30 July 2026 the EU launched a call for tenders to establish up to seven AI Gigafactories across Europe. The initiative is industry-led and backed by up to ten billion euros in EU and national funding, which the Commission expects to unlock at least twenty billion euros of private investment. The facilities are to combine advanced AI processors, software and cloud stacks, high-speed connectivity and energy-efficient data centres, and to give start-ups, scale-ups, SMEs, industry, academia and public authorities access to infrastructure for training, inference and fine-tuning of frontier models. They would sit alongside Europe's nineteen AI Factories. The call closes on 12 November 2026, with awards expected in early 2027.

strand_c.title: New think tank 'Rhine Group' aims to accelerate implementation of Draghi Report recommendations
strand_c.summary: Following Mario Draghi's report on the future of European competitiveness, a new think tank called the Rhine Group has been established to accelerate implementation of its recommendations. It is co-chaired by Draghi and Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, with LSE public policy professor Luis Garicano as executive director, and comprises 54 chief executives, economists, scientists and technology company leaders. The group's stated case is that only four of the world's fifty largest technology companies are European and that Europe is weak across emerging technologies. It argues Europe is in a harder position than when the Draghi report appeared. The item reports formation and stated aims, not any results.

strand_c.title: Event Report: Supporting the Ukrainian Research Ecosystem through International Exchange and Collaboration
strand_c.summary: The satellite event to the ALLEA General Assembly 2026 in Warsaw brought together European academies, Ukrainian institutions, policymakers and the Ukrainian scientific diaspora. Participants reviewed four years of support and argued that preserving Ukraine's research capacity is a strategic investment in Europe's shared scientific future, not only solidarity. Recommendations covered funding schemes, bilateral programmes, collaborative research centres, access to facilities abroad and equipment donation; many were reflected in the Appeal of the ALLEA General Assembly in Support of Ukrainian Science adopted on 28 May 2026. The event marked the official launch of the EFDS Alumni Network, intended as a long-term platform for former fellowship grantees. Outputs are commitments and a new network, not measured results.

strand_c.title: Commission publishes report on Research and Technological Development Activities in 2025
strand_c.summary: The Commission published its annual report on EU research and technological development activities and Horizon Europe monitoring for 2025, focusing this year on sustainable prosperity, competitiveness, strategic autonomy, defence and security alongside the twin transition and international cooperation. Between 2021 and 2025 Horizon Europe received 148,884 eligible proposals. By January 2026, 21,329 had been selected with an estimated 57.4 billion euros of EU contribution, and by end 2025, 52.8 billion euros had been awarded through 19,456 grants. The success rate fell to 14 percent from 15.3 percent, still above the Horizon 2020 average. Around 70 percent of proposals rated fundable could not be financed, a gap of 118.5 billion euros.

strand_c.title: Commission proposes €12,8 billion for Horizon Europe in 2027
strand_c.summary: The European Commission presented a proposed 2027 annual budget of EUR 200 billion. Within it, EUR 13.8 billion is earmarked for research and innovation, of which EUR 12.8 billion is for Horizon Europe. The Commission attributes the slight fall relative to 2026 to a cut in the ITER budget rather than to a reduction in the programme's own ambition. The draft also incorporates the outcome of the mid-term review of 2021-2027 Cohesion policy and encourages Member States to redirect funding towards competitiveness, defence, affordable housing, water resilience and the energy transition, supported by one-off pre-financing and higher co-financing rates. This is a Commission proposal, not an adopted budget.

strand_c.title: Strengthening Europe’s Tech Sovereignty
strand_c.summary: The Commission's tech-sovereignty page sets out a package adopted on 3 June 2026. It contains two legislative proposals, the Chips Act 2.0 and the Cloud and AI Development Act, plus a Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in Energy. The stated rationale is that the EU depends on non-EU suppliers for more than 80 percent of key digital products, services, infrastructure and intellectual property. The page links the package to the AI Continent Action Plan, the Apply AI Strategy, AI Factories and the Quantum Europe Strategy. These are adopted proposals and roadmaps, so the effects described remain intentions rather than measured outcomes.

strand_c.title: Commission proposes tech sovereignty package to strengthen Europe's digital autonomy and resilience
strand_c.summary: On 3 June 2026 the Commission presented a European Technological Sovereignty Package covering semiconductors, artificial intelligence, cloud computing and open source, containing two legislative proposals. The Chips Act 2.0 would expand European semiconductor capacity, especially for advanced AI chips, by speeding up permitting, supporting strategic investments, deepening cooperation with trusted partners and creating an excellence label for semiconductor regions. The Cloud and AI Development Act aims to triple Europe's data-centre capacity within five to seven years and to introduce an EU-wide framework for assessing cloud and AI sovereignty. The package also includes an Open Source Strategy and a roadmap for digitalisation and AI in energy. These are proposals at the start of the legislative process.

strand_c.summary: ALLEA published its statement 'Science Knows No Borders' on 29 June 2026. strand_c.title: Choose Europe for Science
strand_c.summary: Choose Europe for Science is an MSCA pilot action aimed at making European research careers more attractive by tackling precarity and turning brain drain into brain gain. Academic and non-academic organisations recruit postdoctoral researchers with a view to employment beyond the project period, and its stated novelty is that applicants are assessed partly on the longer-term professional prospects they offer. A single legal entity in a Member State or Horizon Europe associated country applies, with associated partners possible. The call budget is 22.5 million euros, capped at 3.5 million per beneficiary, and projects should recruit at least three researchers for up to five years, with MSCA covering the first two to three. Full conditions sit in the 2025 MSCA Work Programme.

strand_c.title: Ukraine bets on research talent and a thriving startup sector

strand_c.title: Experts call for a new approach to Neuro-AI governance
strand_c.summary: On 8 September 2026 the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies released a statement titled 'Governing Neuro-AI: Towards an Infrastructure Approach'. It responds to the convergence of neurotechnology and artificial intelligence, where neurodata can be collected, combined and reused to build AI models across contexts. The EGE argues for a systemic and anticipatory approach, moving the regulatory focus from individual devices and neurodata privacy to the wider infrastructures through which neurodata are collected, processed and reused. strand_c.title: First release of the EuroHPC Federation Platform to streamline access to Europe’s supercomputing resources
strand_c.summary: The EuroHPC Federation Platform went live on 15 April 2026 as a single access point to multiple operational EuroHPC systems, with unified authentication, authorisation and identification. EuroHPC machines each had their own procedures for authentication, resource allocation, job scheduling and software provisioning, which complicated cross-site work. The platform harmonises access through a federated software catalogue while aiming at easier onboarding, greater user awareness of energy efficiency, reduced duplication and high security standards. It is presented as a one-stop shop for researchers, SMEs and public authorities. This is an initial release, so coverage and uptake are not yet evidenced.

strand_c.title: ERA Forum focuses on ERA Act, talent attraction and ERA Policy Agenda implementation
strand_c.summary: The ERA Forum met for its 33rd session in Malta on 9 and 10 June 2026. Timings remain indicative rather than fixed.

strand_c.title: LERU publishes proposal for a framework to help universities navigate defence research
strand_c.summary: On 26 May 2026 the League of European Research Universities published 'Defence Research in European Universities: A Conceptual Framework'. The paper identifies six structural tensions where legitimate institutional values genuinely conflict and argues that existing governance frameworks, designed for an earlier era, are increasingly inadequate. It maps five distinctive European traditions, French, German, British and Dutch, Nordic, and neutral state, to explain why institutions in different legal and historical contexts will reasonably reach different conclusions. Rather than seeking agreement on outcomes, it offers shared vocabulary and analytical tools so each institution can articulate its own position. It also examines the EU dimension, including strategic autonomy frameworks, the European Defence Fund and the blurring of civilian and security research objectives.

strand_c.title: Commission publishes study supporting the Review of the Digital Decade Policy Programme
strand_c.summary: The European Commission released the external study supporting its review of the Digital Decade Policy Programme, covering priorities, targets and indicators on one side and governance and stakeholder engagement on the other. It concluded that the governance framework still works for cooperation between the EU and member states but needs updating against geopolitical, technological and economic change. Current targets were found not to reflect emerging priorities such as cybersecurity, technological sovereignty and resilience, and some indicators need revision. The study also considered investment needs and alignment with the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework. Its recommendations inform, but do not constitute, the Commission's forthcoming review.

strand_c.reader_what: An expert report finds open access progress real but fragmented across member states, with rising publishing charges a structural barrier.
strand_c.reader_why: Fragmented national rules and costs shape what European research is actually readable.
strand_c.reader_more: The European Commission published an independent expert report reviewing open access across all 27 member states and eight non-EU countries. It finds genuine progress but persistent fragmentation: countries differ on legal enforceability, embargo periods, copyright mechanisms, repository requirements and monitoring. The report identifies what works, namely combining legislation, funder mandates and institutional support rather than relying on a single instrument, and notes that mandates tied to research assessment change behaviour while policies without operational support often do not. Rising article processing charges are flagged as a structural barrier that falls hardest on under-resourced institutions, with a call for systematic tracking of that spending.

strand_c.reader_title: Deadlock over new EU spending rules postpones Parliament votes on the next Horizon Europe
strand_c.reader_what: Research committee votes on Horizon Europe and the Competitiveness Fund slipped because the Performance Framework Regulation is unresolved.
strand_c.reader_why: Delay compresses the trilogue window and threatens a 2028 start for the next framework programme.
strand_c.reader_more: Legislative work on the next Horizon Europe and the European Competitiveness Fund has stalled while the European Parliament's budgets committee settles the Performance Framework Regulation, a horizontal set of monitoring rules from the Commission's July 2025 MFF proposal. The disagreement is between the S&D, which wants the regulation applied across all sectoral programmes at once, and the EPP, which opposes that. Committee votes originally set for 10 September were postponed and the plenary vote moved from 5 October to mid-November. Research Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva had said a deal by end-2026 was needed for a 1 January 2028 start. A separate dispute over expert councils governing Pillar 2 also remains open.

strand_c.reader_title: Finland's LUMI AI Factory to host a staged IQM quantum computer built for logical qubits
strand_c.reader_what: CSC will host LUMI-IQ, an IQM superconducting machine delivered in stages from 2027 to 2029.
strand_c.reader_why: Places error-corrected quantum hardware inside a European HPC and AI facility the host institution controls.
strand_c.reader_more: CSC - IT Center for Science in Kajaani will host LUMI-IQ, described as Europe's first superconducting quantum computer designed from the outset to operate with logical qubits. Logical qubits combine several error-prone physical qubits into a more reliable computational unit through quantum error correction. An IQM Halocene H4 system with 150 physical qubits arrives in 2027, with error-correction upgrades in 2028 and a Halocene H5 upgrade in 2029, jointly funded by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking with Finland, Czechia, Norway and Poland. The machine will be integrated with the LUMI AI Factory's classical HPC and AI resources for hybrid workflows. Nothing has been delivered yet, so the announcement sets out a procurement and a schedule rather than an installed capability.

strategic_pathways.reader_title: New MSCA pilot funds longer-term postdoctoral posts to counter research precarity
strategic_pathways.reader_what: A 22.5 million euro MSCA pilot selects institutions partly on the long-term job security they offer researchers.
strategic_pathways.reader_why: Ties EU research funding to employment conditions rather than project output alone.
strategic_pathways.reader_more: Choose Europe for Science is an MSCA pilot action aimed at making European research careers more attractive by tackling precarity and turning brain drain into brain gain. Academic and non-academic organisations recruit postdoctoral researchers with a view to employment beyond the project period, and its stated novelty is that applicants are assessed partly on the longer-term professional prospects they offer. A single legal entity in a Member State or Horizon Europe associated country applies, with associated partners possible. The call budget is 22.5 million euros, capped at 3.5 million per beneficiary, and projects should recruit at least three researchers for up to five years, with MSCA covering the first two to three. Full conditions sit in the 2025 MSCA Work Programme.

dynamic_shocks.title: A security reclassification abruptly narrows access to Europe’s research infrastructures
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on research infrastructures. Separate primary evidence shows that a sudden security reclassification can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of research infrastructures.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for a sudden security reclassification.
Primary evidence contains 2 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
3 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
2 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on research infrastructures for current or planned work.
A sudden security reclassification reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Maintain alternative facilities and access routes for projects that depend on shared infrastructure.
Avoid a single access system becoming the only route into several European facilities.
Use common, targeted screening rules rather than broad restrictions that fragment European access.
watch_for: Research previously treated as open is moved into a more restricted security category.
Different European countries apply materially different access decisions to the same work.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Well supported enough to watch closely, with contextual signals reinforcing rather than carrying the case.

dynamic_shocks.title: A conflict escalation severs Europe’s access to open science and research data
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on open science and research data. Separate primary evidence shows that an armed-conflict escalation can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of open science and research data.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for an armed-conflict escalation.
Primary evidence contains 1 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
2 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
2 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on open science and research data for current or planned work.
An armed-conflict escalation reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: Only one primary retained record currently links the European capability directly to the outside pressure.
The primary direct connection is concentrated in one source, so independent confirmation is still weak.
The primary corpus contains 5 strong sign(s) of substitution, resilience or policy response that could absorb the shock.
Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Separate genuinely sensitive research from ordinary open research instead of using blanket restrictions.
Use common European safeguards so institutions do not create incompatible access rules.
Prepare relocation, remote-access and project-transfer plans before a research corridor closes.
watch_for: A research corridor closes, staff are evacuated, or facilities become inaccessible.
European partners take over work that can no longer be carried out locally.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Plausible, but important parts of the primary trigger or connection still need confirmation.

historical_context.reader_title: A Nordic model for sharing health data across borders
historical_context.reader_what: The VALO project released a collaboration model to enable cross-border secondary use of Nordic health data for research.
historical_context.reader_why: Larger pooled data attracts research and prepares Nordic countries for the European Health Data Space.
historical_context.reader_more: The Value from Nordic Health Data project, funded by the Nordic Council of Ministers, has released a preliminary model for sharing and reusing health data across Nordic borders. The region has unusual advantages: comprehensive population registries, personal identification numbers that allow record linkage, high public trust and a shared emphasis on data protection. These have been underused because regulations are fragmented, access timelines long and GDPR interpreted differently between countries. The model rests on three connected areas, knowledge sharing about systems and structures, research collaboration and statistics, and a coordinating Driver function maintaining strategic alignment and ethical standards. It is framed around how the European Health Data Space will be implemented in the Nordics.

historical_context.reader_title: Organisational similarity drives which European universities collaborate on research
historical_context.reader_what: Doctoral programme capacity is the most stable predictor of European university research ties
historical_context.reader_why: Identifies a lever European funders can use to reduce research fragmentation
historical_context.reader_more: The authors model two collaboration networks among European universities, one built from joint projects and one from co-authored publications, in physical sciences and engineering and in life sciences over 2011-2016. They use exponential random graph models, a statistical technique for networks that tests which organisational attributes predict a tie while controlling for geography. Research capability, measured by the size of doctoral programmes, is the clearest and most stable predictor both of forming ties at all and of choosing similar partners. historical_context.reader_title: Which European regions win Framework Programme funding, and why
historical_context.reader_what: Southern European private sectors attract funding through high proposal intensity, while blue banana universities win through R&D investment.
historical_context.reader_why: Shows cohesion aims and funding outcomes diverging between sectors across EU regions.
historical_context.reader_more: The authors examine why EU Framework Programme funding is distributed so unevenly, moving below the country level to NUTS-2 regions and separating the higher education and private sectors. They analyse EUR 71.6 billion distributed between 2007 and 2020, measuring grant funding per unit of R&D personnel and testing how regional research personnel, R&D investment, research intensity and development level affect it, mediated by the amount of funding requested. In the private sector several southern European regions perform strongly, largely by applying for a great deal. In higher education the advantage lies with the blue banana regions, driven by high R&D investment and research intensity. From FP7 to Horizon 2020 private-sector divergence increased in favour of peripheral regions.

historical_context.reader_point: Abstract During the past decade, responsible research assessment (RRA) has become a major science policy goal to advance responsible research and innovation and open science.

historical_context.metadata_correction_reason: The scanner recorded 2023-10-01 from the issue cover date; OUP and Crossref give the online publication date as 28 November 2023 (issue dated October 2023).
historical_context.reader_title: The legal basis for reforming research assessment in Europe
historical_context.reader_what: Responsible research assessment rests mainly on soft law and self-regulation, with hard law covering only academic freedom and non-discrimination.
historical_context.reader_why: Explains why assessment reform commitments bind loosely and vary between member states.
historical_context.reader_more: The authors ask whether there is a legal foundation for responsible research assessment and what obstacles stand in the way of turning reform into practice. They analyse sources ranging from binding hard law through soft law to self-regulation, at EU level and in Italy as a national case. They find that apart from constitutional and legal provisions on freedom of research, university autonomy, non-discrimination and gender equality, the foundation rests mainly on soft law and policy norms such as Council conclusions and the 2022 Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment, which is explicitly not legally binding. The legal basis is weakest precisely where reform asks institutions to abandon inappropriate practices such as misusing journal impact factors. historical_context.reader_more: The author asks how European integration extends into outer space, taking the Ariane launcher as her case. Jointly built by thirteen countries and heavily subsidised, Ariane has been treated as a symbol of European technological integration since the European Space Agency's founding objective of building a European launcher. Controversies about its future entangle questions of innovation, security and geopolitical power, especially as commercial competitors reshape the sector. Using the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries from science and technology studies, and drawing on two years of fieldwork including interviews and participant observation in the European space sector plus document analysis of space policy reports, she traces which space futures are projected onto Ariane and how they relate to the ideals and tensions of European integration.

historical_context.reader_what: The GREAT project embedded climate surveys in popular mobile games, reaching 130 million players and 200,000 completed responses.
historical_context.reader_why: Shows a workable channel for public engagement with groups formal consultations never reach.
historical_context.reader_more: Most people never take part in a formal climate policy consultation, but many play video games. The EU-funded GREAT project, coordinated from Germany's Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education, tested whether games could open a channel between citizens and policymakers. Working with PlanetPlay and more than 30 studios, it embedded short climate surveys inside popular mobile titles, reaching around 130 million players, with 1.2 million engaging and over 200,000 completing them. The project also ran collaborative dilemma games in Austria, Cyprus and the United Kingdom to generate deeper qualitative discussion. The researchers are candid that large-scale engagement is only half the problem: turning input into policy would need much closer involvement from policymakers.

The centres were funded for five years between 2017 and 2022, with NordForsk joined as funders by the research councils of Norway, Finland and Sweden and Iceland's Rannis. historical_context.reader_title: What the Ukraine war revealed about space as a security domain
historical_context.reader_what: Commercial satellite services proved decisive, blurring military and civilian lines and pushing states toward sovereign space capability.
historical_context.reader_why: Reliance on commercial space assets reshapes what European space capability must provide.
historical_context.reader_more: This Hybrid CoE working paper examines how the space domain has been used and affected during the war in Ukraine, which the authors argue has been used more versatilely than in any previous conflict. Crowdsourced situational awareness from civilians has supported field operations, while satellite-based technologies have become everyday tools for military and civilian users alike, showing that access to space capabilities matters more than owning them. That reliance on commercial assets in military operations blurs the line between military and civilian actors, and advances in satellite technology enable new capability combinations. A major consequence has been the degradation of cooperative spirit in international space programmes, pushing countries toward national and regional activity to secure sovereignty.

historical_context.reader_why: Assessment practice determines whether open science commitments change researcher behaviour.
historical_context.reader_more: Speaking at the Paris Open Science European Conference, the author argues the relationship runs both ways: reforming research assessment is needed to make open science real, but open science has itself been the main driver pushing assessment toward more comprehensive evaluation. She presents the institutional picture from the European University Association's Expert Group on Open Science, which has tracked trends for about a decade through successive surveys of universities. These began in 2014 asking only about open access to publications, added FAIR data, and from 2017 included research assessment. She draws on the two most recent EUA surveys and reports, and also describes the Open Knowledge Action Plan approved at the Open University of Catalonia in 2018 as an institutional example.

historical_context.reader_why: Anchors French and European capability in a contested strategic technology.
historical_context.reader_more: PEPR Quantique is an acceleration national research programme led jointly by CEA, CNRS and Inria, with a budget of EUR 150 million running six years from 2022 to 2028. It is the cornerstone of France's national quantum strategy, supporting academic research from fundamental concepts through to proofs of principle. The page sets out the breadth involved: fundamental and applied physics, theoretical computer science, engineering, mathematics and chemistry, with current challenges including computing capacity, fault tolerance, software architecture, more powerful sensors and hybrid fibre and satellite communication networks. Targeted projects cover new computing paradigms, quantum communication and cryptography, precision metrology and sensing, and cryptography resistant to future quantum attacks, with a twofold challenge of linking fundamental to industrial research and training future talent.
