historical_context.reader_title: European research organisations object to EIC intellectual property rules
historical_context.reader_what: Signatory associations argue EIC Pathfinder and Transition IP provisions conflict with institutional and national rules and deter participation.
historical_context.reader_why: IP terms shape whether European research organisations take part in EIC funding at all.
historical_context.reader_more: Associations of research-performing organisations and knowledge transfer professionals jointly urged the European Commission to apply the standard Horizon Europe intellectual property rules to European Innovation Council Transition and Pathfinder projects, rather than the special provisions then in force. Those provisions grant EIC inventors indefinite, royalty-free access rights for exploitation, with royalties shared only where the employing organisation supports the inventor's exploitation. The signatories argue these terms conflict with institutional, national and regional rules, hindering their members' participation in the EIC, and may undermine their own efforts to maximise exploitation of research results. They tie the argument to the Commission's own knowledge valorisation guiding principles, Council conclusions on the New European Innovation Agenda and a European Parliament report on EIC implementation.

historical_context.reader_title: Place-blind R&D spending is not enough to raise SME innovation across EU regions
historical_context.reader_what: Collaboration matters more than R&D for SME innovation, and its effect varies strongly by regional context.
historical_context.reader_why: Implies EU innovation policy built on a uniform R&D-intensity target misallocates effort in weaker regions.
historical_context.reader_more: EU innovation policy has long been organised around raising R&D investment towards three per cent of GDP. The authors argue this is place-blind, because SME innovation draws on internal R&D, non-R&D inputs and external collaboration, all shaped by location. Using Regional Innovation Scoreboard data covering 220 regions in 22 European countries, they find SMEs in more innovative regions benefit from combining internal R&D, collaboration of all kinds and non-R&D inputs, while SMEs in less innovative regions depend mainly on external sources and especially on collaboration with other firms. Greater public R&D investment does not reliably improve regional SME innovation. They conclude that a more collaboration-based, place-sensitive policy is needed.

historical_context.reader_title: Researcher mobility is stickier and less binary than institutions assume
historical_context.reader_what: Early-career researchers experience a range of sticky-to-stretchy mobility that defies the mobile/immobile split.
historical_context.reader_why: Mobility requirements built on a binary view can penalise researchers whose constraints are structural and gendered.
historical_context.reader_more: Swiss academia has the highest inbound and outbound mobility in Europe and, in line with European Research Area aims, funds scientific mobility and extended research stays as tools for collaboration and excellence. Institutions have simultaneously worried that female academics are less mobile and that local family ties damage their careers. Drawing on 65 semi-structured interviews conducted for two EU research projects with early-career academics from varied backgrounds, the author shows that researchers' own accounts unsettle the traditional and often gendered mobile/immobile dichotomy. Interviewees treat mobility practices as normalised. Using the concept of stickiness, the article describes a graded range of sticky-to-stretchy mobility experiences shaped by both structural conditions and individual circumstances.

historical_context.reader_title: OECD report on precarious postdoctoral careers and how to reduce them
historical_context.reader_what: Precarity among postdoctoral researchers is widespread across OECD systems, worsened but not caused by Covid-19.
historical_context.reader_why: Prolonged precarity narrows who can stay in research, affecting talent retention and the quality of science.
historical_context.reader_more: The report focuses on the research precariat, defined as postdoctoral researchers on fixed-term positions without permanent or continuous employment prospects. It finds precarity widespread across OECD countries and research systems, with Covid-19 aggravating a pre-existing problem rather than creating it. Doctorate attainment rose about twenty-five per cent across the OECD between 2014 and 2019 while secure academic positions did not keep pace, producing long postdoctoral periods on short-term contracts. It reports detrimental effects on wellbeing, opaque selection procedures, concerns about workforce diversity, and women disproportionately leaving at the early-to-mid career transition. It argues a publish-or-perish culture imperils research quality. It offers nine recommendations spanning working conditions, professional development, equal opportunities, funding and human resource links, mobility, evidence and governance.

historical_context.reader_title: How foresight brought sustainability goals into EU research policy
historical_context.reader_what: The BOHEMIA foresight exercise placed the SDGs in Horizon Europe, but delivery depends on reflexive governance.
historical_context.reader_why: Without sustained reflexivity in implementation, sustainability goals risk remaining a framing rather than a steer.
historical_context.reader_more: The authors note that the Commission's Horizon Europe proposal was the first EU framework programme proposal prepared using a major foresight exercise, the BOHEMIA project, which brought the Sustainable Development Goals into the preparation debate. Drawing on transition management, they argue that success in pursuing the goals depends on the reflexivity of governance, and that foresight is how reflexivity is built in. They set out four dimensions of change that policy must relate to: emerging technological developments, new forms of use and institutional conditions, changes in the global context, and consequences for normative orientations. They assess how far BOHEMIA raised reflexivity in preparing the proposal, and argue that reflexive effort is needed throughout implementation, not only in design. Whether the Commission delivers that, they leave open.

historical_context.reader_more: Some European politicians have held up Chinese industrial policy, and firms such as CRRC and Huawei, as examples to follow. The author argues this ignores the downsides of an approach that works only under China's hybrid state capitalism, where market forces are welcome only when they serve strategic goals. Market distortions, duplicated local initiatives, overcapacity and rising debt are tolerated because the party controls everything, at the cost of entrepreneurial vitality. historical_context.reader_what: The Czech Evaluation Methodology allocated institutional research funding by purely quantitative output counts, creating instability and hidden politics.
historical_context.reader_why: A cautionary case for European countries designing performance-based research funding systems.
historical_context.reader_more: After post-communist restructuring, the Czech Republic introduced a performance-based system that counted publications, patents and prototypes to set institutional funding. Intended to depoliticise allocation, raise productivity and ensure accountability, it evolved into a mechanistic “coffee mill”. They compare it with systems in the UK, Norway, Finland, Poland and elsewhere.

historical_context.summary: The chapter studies the European Research Infrastructure Consortium (ERIC), a legal form created by the EU for jointly run research infrastructures. Its case is BBMRI, the pan-European biobanking infrastructure financed by the EU and participating states. The notes show the analysis engages EU constitutional law and the fragmented national rules on consent and ethics review for biobank research. The research was done within the Swedish BBMRI node.
historical_context.relevance_note: Historical evidence on EU research-infrastructure governance (ERIC, BBMRI).

lenses.passage: Aim of the initiative The objective of Chips Act 2 .0 is to increase the competitiveness of the European ecosystem to strengthen technological sovereignty and resilience and enhanc e crisis preparedness to ensure the EU’s security of supply and economic security. Building on the first Chips Act, the initiative aims to address these weaknesses and challenges with the objectives of: • Enhancing the EU’s capacity and security of supply in mainstream and advanced semiconductors, including AI chips; • Developing a strong user market across key industry sectors; • Increasing intelligence capabilities for crisis preparedness and response.
